lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the state and its limits
lead.head: Bumping into the invisible state

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 25

body: Ajay Shah was in a spot­less of­fice, busy talk­ing, when he turned abruptly to fetch his com­puter from a room. He walked straight into a glass wall wiped so clean that noth­ing showed it was there. {025-S01}
Amit Varma, after a joke at his friend’s ex­pense, saw a metaphor. The state, he said, is “like that in­vis­i­ble fist”: we don’t see it, and it gets in our way when we least ex­pect it.
Shah agreed. “The state is om­nipresent, it in­vis­i­bly re­shapes our life and once in a while it slams into your face.”
The episode set out to make that wall vis­i­ble: why the state ex­ists, what it costs, and how far it should reach.
## The price of rights

Varma began with rights. They mean some­thing only when they are de­fended, and de­fend­ing them needs a state with a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence. So we give up some rights to pro­tect the rest, a para­dox at the heart of lib­er­al­ism.

His claim went fur­ther than say­ing that some state ac­tions are vi­o­lent. “I mean the ex­is­tence of the state it­self is at its core vi­o­lence,” he said. Nobody would pay taxes un­less forced to, and the state threat­ens to im­prison those who don’t.

Taxes, di­rect and in­di­rect, may take a third of your in­come. “Between January and April every year, you don’t work for your­self, you work for the state,” Varma said. We are all, in his phrase, in “part time slav­ery”. {025-C05}

None of this makes the state il­le­git­i­mate, he stressed: we need it. But every ide­ol­ogy, com­mu­nist, lib­er­tar­ian or so­cial demo­crat, must an­swer the same ques­tion. When is this vi­o­lence jus­ti­fied, and why? {025-C04}
## Scope ver­sus strength

The sec­ond frame came from Francis Fukuyama’s *State Building*. Instead of ar­gu­ing over big states and small ones, Varma said, ask how many things a state tries to do, and how well it does them. {025-C10}

On Fukuyama’s map, Sierra Leone does lit­tle and does it badly; the Soviet Union did ev­ery­thing, with mid­dling strength. Varma wants lim­ited scope and mas­sive strength. India, he ar­gued, is the re­verse: it med­dles in bed­rooms and busi­nesses and fails at its core jobs.

Shah re­jected the mid­dle-class idea of a strong state as one that can jail the pow­er­ful or pass a law overnight. Strength should mean com­pe­tence: a polio cam­paign that reaches every child within a year or two.
Liberal democ­racy, he said, is meant to be slow. Power is dis­persed and many peo­ple can veto, and that slow­ness is the de­sign, not a fail­ure of it.
## The tortoise’s pace

The same pa­tience ap­plies to growth. Many hope that 7 per cent per capita growth would bring India within spit­ting dis­tance of America in 30 years. Shah said such growth, sus­tained that long, has es­sen­tially never hap­pened.
“That’s a bad dream, that’s a wrong ob­jec­tive to pur­sue,” he said. {025-C14}

Asked once whether India should be a tiger or an ele­phant, Shah chose the tor­toise, chip­ping away at sus­tained growth. The boom after 1991, Varma said, came from free­ing parts of the econ­omy so that peo­ple could dis­cover pos­i­tive-sum trades, not from growth tar­gets.
Varma tied Shah’s phrase, “dis­cover, not de­sign”, to Adam Ferguson’s idea of progress through “human ac­tion, but not human de­sign”.
Shah, sign­ing off, counted the an­i­mals the episode had pro­duced: a cat, a dog, a pig, a tiger, an ele­phant, a tor­toise and a hare.

second.label: Law and certainty
second.head: Easy come, easy repeal
second.deck: Ajay Shah heard a boast about decisiveness as a warning about certainty

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the law enacted by the day after

body: Ajay Shah was once dis­cussing se­cu­ri­ties law with a pol­i­cy­maker in the UAE. The of­fi­cial waved his fist and made an offer: give him the cor­rect se­cu­ri­ties law to­mor­row, and he would have it en­acted by the day after. {025-S06}

Shah drew the op­po­site les­son. “In my mind, I thought that there is then no cer­tainty at all,” he said. A law that can be passed overnight can be changed overnight, leav­ing “com­plete legal risk”.

If there is any fric­tion­less path for a strong state to push out new leg­is­la­tion, Shah ar­gued, the leg­is­la­tion means noth­ing. {#frictionless} A healthy so­ci­ety has checks and bal­ances, with many peo­ple in­volved in every de­ci­sion and no strong­man able to bull­doze through.

quote.text: Because if a law can be en­acted to­mor­row, it can be reen­acted the day after.

third.head: Rote players, rare masters

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the poker stable

body: In his years as a pro­fes­sional poker player, Amit Varma saw many pros start out in a “sta­ble”. A suc­cess­ful player, who could only play so many hands him­self, would stake a group of play­ers and coach them. {025-S02}

The coach­ing was me­chan­ics: with twenty big blinds, here is your reshove range. Players mem­o­rised it and played cor­rectly, “but they’re not think­ing from first prin­ci­ples and fig­ur­ing out shit them­selves,” Varma said.
Only a very small share of the win­ners worked things out. Varma was al­ways ask­ing why.

Ajay Shah of­fered an engineer’s ver­sion: a tech­ni­cian trained on one air con­di­tioner can re­pair it, but with­out ther­mo­dy­nam­ics can­not rein­vent it. Hence his praise for the lib­eral arts, in some ways “the most use­less thing in the world”, and the best kind of ed­u­ca­tion. {025-C01}

p2.title: The state of the state
p2.deck: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah, from first principles, on why the state exists and how far it should reach

quote.text: In some ways the most use­less thing in the world is the lib­eral arts ed­u­ca­tion. You’re ab­so­lutely not job ready.

box.title: A slim book with a red cover
box.text: Francis Fukuyama’s *State Building* is a slim book, Amit Varma said, and ev­ery­one should read it. It swaps the big-state, small-state de­bate for two ques­tions: how much a state does, and how well. {025-R11}

sections.label: The method
sections.head: Ask why, then ask again
sections.caption: mechanics and first principles
body: Ajay Shah opened with a ten­sion. He had re­cently writ­ten about pub­lic pol­icy in the air­line in­dus­try, a deep dive into one ex­am­ple. {#airline} Is it bet­ter to go one prac­ti­cal case at a time, he asked, or to learn gen­eral prin­ci­ples in their own right?

Amit Varma saw two ten­sions. The first is be­tween me­chan­ics and prin­ci­ples: his poker col­leagues mem­o­rised what to play, while he kept ask­ing why. Asking why all the time, he con­ceded, is a bit cum­ber­some.

The sec­ond is about ex­plain­ing. A story grabs at­ten­tion, but the prin­ci­ple it car­ries is often “adrift in space” and eas­ily for­got­ten. A frame­work of first prin­ci­ples and root causes can be ap­plied to ev­ery­thing, and its flaws are easy to find and dis­cuss. {025-C02}
## Economics in ev­ery­thing

That is why Varma loves eco­nom­ics, which some call the dis­mal sci­ence. For him it is the study of human be­hav­iour, and he finds scarcity and in­cen­tives in the best of lit­er­a­ture, art and music.

Shah took it to ed­u­ca­tion. Someone trained on one air con­di­tioner can re­pair it; with­out ther­mo­dy­nam­ics, he will not be ready for the next wave of heat pumps. India, Shah said, val­orises job-ready vo­ca­tional ed­u­ca­tion too much. {025-C01}
~ Both hosts value the hu­man­i­ties, Varma added, but uni­ver­si­ties pro­vide them badly, so we must ed­u­cate our­selves through books, movies and art.

quote.text: In some ways the most use­less thing in the world is the lib­eral arts ed­u­ca­tion. You’re ab­so­lutely not job ready.

sections.label: Framework one
sections.head: The mafia with a monopoly
sections.caption: the state as violence
body: Rights, Amit Varma said, have mean­ing only when they are de­fended. That needs a state with a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence, so we give up some of our rights for the state to exist: the great lib­eral para­dox. {025-C03}

We have nor­malised the state so much, he ar­gued, that we for­get its ex­is­tence is it­self an act of vi­o­lence. Nobody would pay taxes un­less forced. The state, he said, is like a mo­nop­oly mafia that holds you at ran­som. {#mafia}
That does not make it il­le­git­i­mate. Varma rec­om­mended Robert Nozick’s “great book”, *Anarchy, State, and Utopia*, but was clear: “I’m say­ing we need the state.”
## Who re­ally pays

Nor is the cost borne only by the rich. The claim that only 3 per cent of Indians pay taxes, Varma said, is “ab­so­lute non­sense”. The beg­gar at the traf­fic sig­nal pays tax when she buys tea. {025-C06}
Count di­rect and in­di­rect taxes and a third of your in­come may go to the state, he said: from January to April we work for it, in “part time slav­ery”. {025-C05}
You want a space pro­gramme? “It is not money com­ing from the air,” Varma said. “Your do­mes­tic help is pay­ing for it.”
~ Every ide­ol­ogy, he said, dif­fers on one cen­tral ques­tion: when is this vi­o­lence jus­ti­fied, and why? Acknowledge that, and “where you stand is kind of where you stand”. {025-C04}

quote.text: Whatever the state does, it does through vi­o­lence. And there­fore you have to jus­tify that

sections.label: The other wing
sections.head: Rules without a budget
sections.caption: the two channels of state coercion
body: Ajay Shah of­fered a his­tor­i­cal bench­mark. The British taxes that kicked off Gandhiji’s Dandi March, he said, were “mod­est and de­cent” com­pared with the lev­els of tax­a­tion in in­de­pen­dent India. {025-C07}
Then he split the state’s power into two chan­nels. One com­pels peo­ple to pay money, which the gov­ern­ment spends. The other tells them di­rectly what they may not do, on pain of pun­ish­ment.
The first chan­nel has a check. Revenue is hard to raise, ru­pees are fun­gi­ble, peo­ple hate pay­ing, and the bud­get process brings some com­mon sense. The sec­ond has no bud­get at all. {025-C08}
## Hundreds of agen­cies

“There is no sin­gle state­ment that de­tails and doc­u­ments all the acts of state co­er­cion,” Shah said. Hundreds of agen­cies in­tro­duce one new co­er­cion every day, and we have nor­malised the loss of free­dom. {#agencies}

Amit Varma linked this to Subhashish Bhadra’s book *Caged Tiger*. America’s con­sti­tu­tion, born of peo­ple flee­ing per­se­cu­tion, pro­tects the peo­ple from the state. India’s, writ­ten amid the vi­o­lence of Partition, pro­tects the state from the peo­ple. {025-C09}
~ The re­sult, Varma said, is a mind­set in which we exist for the state’s sake, to pay taxes and be sub­jects, and mis­sion creep fol­lows.

quote.text: Year after year, the state just lay­ers on more and more and more co­er­cion and no­body keeps track of it.

art.caption: Amit Varma on the two channels of state coercion

sections.label: Framework two
sections.head: Do less, but do it well
sections.caption: scope and strength
body: Amit Varma’s sec­ond frame­work came from Francis Fukuyama. Too often, he said, the de­bate is re­duced to “big state bad, small state good”. {#bigstate}

Instead, think in two di­men­sions. Scope is ev­ery­thing the state at­tempts, from de­fence and law and order to tem­ples, pil­grim­age sub­si­dies and space pro­grammes. Strength, what econ­o­mists call state ca­pac­ity, is how well it does those things.
Sierra Leone is low on both and might as well not exist as a state. The Soviet Union had mas­sive scope and mid­dling strength. Varma’s ideal is lim­ited scope and mas­sive strength. {025-C10}
## Too much, too badly
India, he said, is the op­po­site. To set up a busi­ness in Delhi, he once read, you need more li­cences than to get a gun. {#gun}

The state in­ter­feres in everybody’s bed­rooms and busi­ness and stops so­ci­ety from solv­ing its own prob­lems, yet fails at what it should do. Except for the priv­i­leged elite, Varma said, “there is no rule of law in India”. {#nolaw}
~ What the hosts want is the op­po­site: a state that does much less, but does it supremely well. Not a big state, Varma said, but a strong one.

quote.text: The ideal state, what I be­lieve, is a state where the scope is lim­ited and the strength is mas­sive.

sections.label: The strong state
sections.head: Strong, as in capable
sections.caption: strength as competence
body: Ajay Shah wor­ries about the Indian mid­dle class’s ad­mi­ra­tion for a strong state. One ver­sion is a state that can grab the most pow­er­ful peo­ple in the coun­try and put them in jail. {025-C11} The other is a leader who an­nounces a new law overnight. Both, he said, are wrong.

Strength should mean com­pe­tence: han­dling COVID vac­ci­na­tion so that as few peo­ple as pos­si­ble die in a sec­ond wave, or reach­ing every child with polio vac­cine within one or two years. {#polio}
Liberal democ­racy dis­perses power, with checks, bal­ances and many ve­toes. That makes it “ap­pear slow and sham­bolic, and that’s a fea­ture, not a bug,” Shah said. {025-C12}
## Ends and means
Amit Varma agreed that strong should mean ro­bust. Rules should be framed so that even the most heinous strong­man who comes to power can do only lim­ited dam­age.
His he­roes of the free­dom strug­gle, Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Ganesh Agarkar, Ranade and Gopal Krishna Gokhale, were lib­eral in their ends and con­ser­va­tive in their means. {025-C13}
~ Change, for them, came through en­gage­ment, dis­course and di­a­logue. Hoping for some­one to seize power and im­pose lib­er­al­ism, Varma said, is not lib­er­al­ism at all.

quote.text: If today some­body can come and im­pose lib­er­al­ism, to­mor­row some­body can come and lock you up and send you into gu­lags.

art.caption: Amit Varma on strength as competence

quote.text: So it is very im­por­tant to see a healthy so­ci­ety as one where there are checks and bal­ances, and then in­evitably the state will be slow, will be de­lib­er­a­tive, it will be con­sul­ta­tive

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Mad sects, two doors, sandstone elephants and a patient tortoise

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the strange origins of the secular state
stories.head: Mad sects and the secular state
body: In the early years of American po­lit­i­cal think­ing, Ajay Shah said, there was a very beau­ti­ful de­bate. It be­gins with the peo­ple who built the coun­try. {025-S05}

In Europe, Catholic and Protestant churches ran a reg­i­mented re­li­gion and per­se­cuted peo­ple who wanted to do de­viant things. Shah did not mean athe­ists. He meant sects cra­zier than main­line European re­li­gion would allow. Many of them fled and es­tab­lished them­selves in America.
“So there’s a very deep idea in America that there should be free­dom to pur­sue your own mad­ness,” he said.

Nobody was think­ing of a post-religious world. The sects were say­ing: don’t mess with me, let me be. Separation of church and state was meant to make room for them, not to open a path to sec­u­lar­i­sa­tion and athe­ism, which is how the 20th cen­tury worked out.

That raised a ques­tion Americans took se­ri­ously. Suppose 20, 100 or 200 peo­ple de­cide to live in a com­mune with a bound­ary wall around it. Which of the state’s rules may they sus­pend? {#commune}
Some must hold ev­ery­where, Shah said. The IPC pro­hibits mur­der, and you should not be able to cre­ate a com­mune within which mur­der is le­git­i­mate. {#murder}
In America, he said, you can cre­ate a new city or a new town­ship, with your own rules to a sig­nif­i­cant ex­tent. Shah called this a great source of en­ergy for the American po­lit­i­cal project.
~ “I think we in India would ben­e­fit from think­ing in these ways,” he said.
stories.why: The sec­u­lar state began as a way of leav­ing re­li­gious odd­balls alone. How far a com­mu­nity may set its own rules is a ques­tion, Shah ar­gued, that India too should take se­ri­ously.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on America’s mad religious sects

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a rule book nobody can obey
stories.head: One door, many doors, no way out
body: In an early episode of *The Seen and the Unseen*, the restau­ra­teur Madhu Menon walked Amit Varma through the plethora of li­cences a restau­rant in Bangalore needed. {025-S04}
The ex­cise de­part­ment, want­ing to see how much al­co­hol came in and went out, al­lowed only one door. The fire safety de­part­ment re­quired mul­ti­ple doors.

No restau­rant could obey both. “You’re break­ing the law no mat­ter what the hell you do,” Varma said. Restaurateurs any­where in India, he added, are so busy pay­ing thirty or forty bribes a month that it be­comes in­cred­i­bly hard to op­er­ate. {#bribes}
~ He called it one ran­dom ex­am­ple of a state whose scope is too vast: it in­ter­feres ev­ery­where and stops so­ci­ety from solv­ing its own prob­lems.
stories.why: A state that tries to do too much writes rules that can­not all be obeyed, so every hon­est busi­ness be­comes a law­breaker by de­fault, and the bribe be­comes a run­ning cost. {025-R12}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the restaurant with one door

stories.kicker: Amit Varma reads from an old list of state spending
stories.head: Sixty-two elephants and a bill
body: On his old blog, *India Uncut*, Amit Varma kept a sec­tion called *Where Your Taxes Go*. It ran past num­ber eighty and, in his words, “just kind of went on for­ever”. {#eighty}

He read out some en­tries. Moustache al­lowances. Educating and re­ha­bil­i­tat­ing mon­keys. Overpaying for con­doms. Policing par­rots. Salaries for fake mu­nic­i­pal em­ploy­ees who don’t exist. Golf bug­gies for the army.

Then stat­ues, hun­dreds and thou­sands of them, for who­ever you fancy. “Sixty-two sand­stone ele­phants is what I see on my list,” Varma said, along with the reg­u­la­tion of skirt hem­lines. {025-S03}
~ The point was not only waste. Every item, he ar­gued, was paid for with money the state takes by force, in­clud­ing from the poor­est of the poor.
stories.why: An ab­surd line item is a moral ques­tion as well as a waste: each one is paid for with money col­lected under co­er­cion, and that cost falls on the poor­est too.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on where your taxes go

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s answer at a literature festival
stories.head: Not a tiger, not an elephant
body: At the Orange City Literature Festival, some­one in the au­di­ence asked Ajay Shah about his dream for India. Should it be a tiger or an ele­phant? {025-S07}
“I want us to be the tor­toise,” Shah an­swered: chip away for long years and get sus­tained growth. “The magic is sus­tained growth.”

India, he said, has in­stead had 20 years of high growth, from 1991 to 2011, and done badly there­after. {#hare} The UK and the United States chugged away for a hun­dred years at mod­est growth rates, with de­cency, con­sul­ta­tion and fewer mis­takes.

~ Amit Varma at last un­der­stood Shah’s talk of a thirty-year sprint. Tortoises can live two or three hun­dred years, the hosts reck­oned. “So for them, thirty year sprint kind of makes sense,” Varma said. {#sprint}
stories.why: Decency, con­sul­ta­tion and fewer mis­takes, kept up over decades, beat a heroic sprint, in Shah’s view. He said 7 per cent per capita growth for thirty years has es­sen­tially never hap­pened in world his­tory. {#never}
stories.postscript: Shah sug­gested the tor­toise lis­tens to *The Seen and the Unseen*. Varma said hares hear it at dou­ble speed. {025-J04}

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 25. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Mahatma Gandhi (Elliott & Fry, public domain); Francis Fukuyama (Gobierno de Chile, CC BY 2.0); Dadabhai Naoroji (R.M. Richardson & Co, public domain); Rabindranath Tagore (Generalstabens litografiska anstalt, public domain); Robert Nozick (Libertarian Review, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Open Library.

shelf.title: The policy questions around airlines
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It is a deep dive into a sin­gle in­dus­try.

shelf.title: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why academia has drifted away from real-world prob­lems: jour­nal-based pro­mo­tion and de­part­men­tal in­cen­tives nar­row every dis­ci­pline, fil­ter out cre­ative mav­er­icks and leave aca­demics writ­ing for each other.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: Every Act of Government Is an Act of Violence
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s core claim that the state runs on co­er­cion, start­ing with taxes, so every state ac­tion car­ries a moral cost that has to be jus­ti­fied; it is why he ranks spend­ing on in­no­va­tion below the rule of law and basic in­fra­struc­ture.

shelf.title: Your maid funds Unani (2007)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It takes apart the myth that only about 3% of Indians pay taxes.

shelf.title: Taxes Should Be Used for Governance, Not Politics
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It con­tin­ues the episode’s ar­gu­ment that be­cause taxes are taken by force, how they are spent has to be jus­ti­fied.

shelf.title: Where Your Taxes Go (India Uncut series)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A mem­o­rable cat­a­logue, from mous­tache al­lowances to sixty-two sand­stone ele­phants, of what co­erced money ends up pay­ing for.

shelf.title: Anarchy, State, and Utopia
shelf.creator: Robert Nozick
shelf.why: He calls it a ‘great book’ and rec­om­mends it as the place to en­gage se­ri­ously with the ques­tion of an­ar­chy ver­sus the state.

shelf.title: Caged Tiger: How Too Much Government Is Holding Indians Back
shelf.creator: Subhashish Bhadra
shelf.why: Bhadra’s frame that con­sti­tu­tions are prod­ucts of their cir­cum­stances: America’s was built to pro­tect peo­ple from the state, while India’s, drafted amid tur­moil and frag­men­ta­tion, cen­tralised power to pro­tect the state from the peo­ple and paid only lip ser­vice to free­dom.

shelf.title: Subhashish Bhadra on Our Dysfunctional State (Episode 333 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Subhashish Bhadra
shelf.why: Subhashish Bhadra on India’s over­reach­ing state, built to rule rather than to serve: the longer con­ver­sa­tion be­hind his book Caged Tiger.

shelf.title: State Building
shelf.creator: Francis Fukuyama
shelf.why: A slim book that re­places the vague ‘big state ver­sus small state’ de­bate with two di­men­sions: how much a state tries to do and how well it does it.

shelf.title: Restaurant Regulations in India (Episode 18 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Madhu Menon
shelf.why: Madhu Menon on how restau­rant reg­u­la­tion in India works as an op­por­tu­nity for rent-seeking: an over­reach­ing state makes hon­est busi­ness im­pos­si­ble and bribes un­avoid­able.

shelf.title: Going from strong as in scary to strong as in capable
shelf.creator: Suyash Rai and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It sets out the dis­tinc­tion Ajay makes in the episode: India should want strength mean­ing com­pe­tence, not strength mean­ing the power to jail any­one or pass any law overnight.

shelf.title: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (Episode 237 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay on what 1991 achieved and left un­done (fac­tor mar­kets, agri­cul­ture), and how free­ing parts of the econ­omy set off the dis­cov­ery and trade be­hind India’s growth spurt.

shelf.title: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Despite the title, an eco­nomic his­tory of India told through the lens of free­dom: the boom after 1869, Nehru’s Fabian so­cial­ism, the lost years from the 1962 war to the Emergency, and the open­ing-up that lifted mil­lions out of poverty.

shelf.title: Essays on Nationalism
shelf.creator: Rabindranath Tagore
shelf.why: A slim, beau­ti­ful book of deep and time­less ideas: Tagore sup­ported Indian in­de­pen­dence yet saw na­tion­al­ism as toxic who­ever wielded it.

shelf.title: The Libertarian Reader
shelf.creator: David Boaz
shelf.why: It col­lects es­says by lib­eral thinkers such as Milton Friedman and Friedrich Hayek, a good dis­til­la­tion of many strands of thought.

shelf.title: What is Libertarianism? (Episode 117 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with David Boaz
shelf.why: A chance to hear Boaz dis­cuss the ideas be­hind the book in con­ver­sa­tion.

shelf.title: The Origins of Political Order
shelf.creator: Francis Fukuyama
shelf.why: He calls the two vol­umes mag­is­te­rial.

shelf.title: Political Order and Political Decay
shelf.creator: Francis Fukuyama
shelf.why: It com­pletes Fukuyama’s his­tory of the state’s evo­lu­tion and helps you see the state-society re­la­tion­ship more clearly.

shelf.title: Kashi Ka Assi
shelf.creator: Kashinath Singh
shelf.why: A line from Kashinath Singh’s book, about play­ing your har­mo­nium while the world goes to hell, gives Amit his stance on so­cial media: block the toxic ac­counts and build a feed of the finest minds.

shelf.title: Pune Public Policy Festival (January 19-20, 2024)
shelf.why: A fes­ti­val (and the show’s spon­sor) that brings young pro­fes­sion­als to­gether with bu­reau­crats, econ­o­mists and thinkers to de­bate trade-offs such as en­vi­ron­ment ver­sus growth and tech­nol­ogy ver­sus pri­vacy; Amit likes that it pulls pol­icy dis­cus­sion back to Pune, once called the Oxford of the East.

laughs.text: Amit, after Ajay’s crash into a spot­less glass wall: ‘in terms of clar­ity, there is some­thing that is out there that can match the clar­ity of your prose. So, you know, com­pli­ment to both you and the glass wall.’

Ajay to a com­menter who said he was too lazy to work things out him­self: ‘So you, gen­tle reader, how dare you be lazy? Your im­mor­tal soul de­serves bet­ter. Get off your butt and start by read­ing a slim book.’
Amit, when Ajay rec­om­mends Tagore: ‘my heart fills with joy that you named my fel­low Bengali Robida, and I al­most feel like you’re flirt­ing with me.’

Amit fi­nally un­der­stands Ajay’s ‘thirty-year sprint’: tor­toises live for cen­turies, so for them 30 years re­ally is a sprint. The tor­toise, he imag­ines, lis­tens to Hindustani clas­si­cal. Ajay adds The Seen and the Unseen, and Amit runs with it: ‘which is often heard by hares at dou­ble speed, which is also per­fectly fine. We cater to hares, we cater to tor­toises, and we cater to some human be­ings.’

David Boaz, read out by Amit: ‘Conservatives want to be your dad, telling you what to do and what not to do. Liberals want to be your mommy, feed­ing you, tuck­ing you in and wip­ing your nose. Libertarians want to treat you as an adult.’ Amit clar­i­fies that Boaz means American wel­fare-state lib­er­als, and urges lis­ten­ers to drop la­bels and think about prin­ci­ples.
